hints: Start by tracing both curves from time 0. What happens immediately after the glucose drink is taken in each person?
Now compare the two lines like with like - think about starting level, height and steepness of the peak, and what happens between 1 h and 3 h.
To earn full credit you need numbers. Pick paired values with units from the axes, for example peak values and 3 h values.
walkthrough:
See the common rise**
Both curves go up after time 0 because glucose from the drink is absorbed from the small intestine into the blood. That is the first shared pattern to state.

Spot the diabetic difference at the start and peak**
The diabetic person starts higher at about $150 \text{ mg } 100\text{cm}^{-3}$ compared to about $110 \text{ mg } 100\text{cm}^{-3}$ in the non-diabetic. The diabetic then shows a steeper rise to a higher peak of about $205-210 \text{ mg } 100\text{cm}^{-3}$, while the non-diabetic peaks lower at about $145-150 \text{ mg } 100\text{cm}^{-3}$ at about 0.6-0.7 h.

Contrast the fall and recovery**
In the non-diabetic the concentration falls quickly to a slight dip of about $95 \text{ mg } 100\text{cm}^{-3}$ at 1 h, then levels back to about $110 \text{ mg } 100\text{cm}^{-3}$ by 3 h. In the diabetic it falls only very slowly and does not return to normal, staying at about $175-180 \text{ mg } 100\text{cm}^{-3}$ at 3 h.

Final answer: Blood glucose rises in both after the drink. Diabetic is always higher, with higher peak and steeper rise, and falls only slowly, still high at 3 h while non-diabetic returns to near normal. e.g. diabetic peaks at approx. 208 mg 100cm-3 at 0.7 h and is still approx. 178 mg 100cm-3 at 3 h, non-diabetic peaks at approx. 148 mg 100cm-3 and falls to approx. 95 mg 100cm-3 at 1 h then approx. 110 mg 100cm-3 at 3 h.

hints: Think about which organ both detects high blood glucose and then secretes the hormone to correct it.
walkthrough:
Link detector to effector**
Blood glucose is monitored by cells that can then release insulin. Those are the beta cells clustered in the islets of Langerhans in the pancreas. The hypothalamus also contains glucoreceptors, so either location is accepted.
Final answer: Beta cells of the islets of Langerhans in the pancreas (accept hypothalamus).

hints: Remember the general homeostatic rule where a change triggers a response that reverses the original change back toward the set point.
walkthrough:
Name the stabilising loop**
A rise in blood glucose triggers insulin release, which lowers glucose, which then switches off further insulin release. Because the response reverses the stimulus, this is negative feedback control.
Final answer: Negative feedback.

hints: Look at the substrates in Fig. 7.2. Enzyme A acts on glucose to make hydrogen peroxide, enzyme B uses hydrogen peroxide to make colour.
Recall the standard paired enzymes used for glucose testing - one oxidises glucose, the other breaks down peroxide while oxidising a dye.
walkthrough:
Match enzyme to reaction**
Enzyme A converts glucose in urine to gluconic acid plus hydrogen peroxide, so it is an oxidase acting on glucose: glucose oxidase.

Follow the peroxide**
Enzyme B uses hydrogen peroxide plus colourless chromogen to form water plus coloured chromogen, so it is the peroxide-using enzyme: hydrogen peroxidase.
Final answer: A - glucose oxidase; B - (hydrogen) peroxidase.

hints: Think about what a blood sample with an electronic meter gives you compared with just looking at a colour change in urine.
Now think the opposite way - what is easier, cheaper and less painful about dipping a stick into urine?
walkthrough:
Advantage of the biosensor**
A biosensor works on a tiny drop of blood and gives a fast numerical value within seconds. It measures current blood glucose directly and is more accurate, precise and quantitative than matching a colour by eye.

Advantage of the dipstick**
A dipstick only needs urine, so there is no needle prick, no pain and less risk of infection. It is also simple to use and cheap, useful for quick screening.

Final answer: Biosensor: rapid / immediate reading, more accurate / precise / quantitative / numerical / sensitive, shows current blood glucose, re-usable. Dipstick: non-invasive / painless / less risk of infection / easy to use / cheap.

hints: Start where insulin first acts - what does it bind to and on which target organs?
Think about how muscle and fat cells are made more permeable to glucose and how liver cells trap glucose inside.
Once more glucose is inside cells, what useful pathways can it be pushed into for energy use and storage as glycogen?
Remember insulin does not only switch things on - what breakdown processes does it switch off?
Finish the story by linking all these effects to the overall change in blood glucose concentration.
walkthrough:
Binding to target cells**
Insulin is the signal for plenty of glucose. It binds to specific glycoprotein receptors on the cell surface membranes of liver cells, skeletal muscle cells and adipose tissue. Binding is what triggers all the later changes.

Getting glucose into cells**
In muscle and adipose cells, insulin causes vesicles containing GLUT4 transporter proteins to fuse with the membrane, so permeability to glucose rises and more glucose enters by facilitated diffusion. In liver cells it increases uptake and the enzyme glucokinase phosphorylates glucose to glucose phosphate, trapping it inside.

Using and storing glucose**
Inside cells more glucose is respired to release ATP. Insulin also activates glycogen synthase, so excess glucose is converted to glycogen in liver and muscle. That process is glycogenesis.

Stopping glucose release**
At the same time insulin inhibits breakdown pathways. It decreases glycogenolysis to glucose, decreases lipolysis in adipose, and decreases gluconeogenesis from amino acids and glycerol in the liver. It also promotes conversion of excess to lipid / triglyceride for long term storage.

Overall result**
Because uptake, respiration and storage are increased while release is decreased, glucose is removed from the blood faster than it is added, so blood glucose concentration falls back toward normal.

Final answer: Insulin binds to receptors on liver, muscle and adipose cells. Causes GLUT4 channels to be added to muscle and adipose cell membranes, increasing glucose uptake by facilitated diffusion; increases glucose uptake and phosphorylation by glucokinase in liver. Increases respiration of glucose, activates glycogen synthase causing glycogenesis, stimulates conversion to lipid / triglyceride / fatty acid, inhibits glycogenolysis, lipolysis and gluconeogenesis. Blood glucose concentration decreases.
